chunks.title: Create the base revenue measure
chunks.prompt: Write a reusable measure named Total Revenue that sums Sales[Revenue].
chunks.solution: Total Revenue = SUM(Sales[Revenue])
hints: Use SUM around the numeric revenue column.

chunks.title: Ignore product filters
chunks.prompt: Create Revenue All Products by recalculating Total Revenue while removing filters from Product.
chunks.solution: Revenue All Products = CALCULATE([Total Revenue], ALL(Product))
hints: ALL(Product) removes filters from the Product table.

chunks.title: Respect report selections
chunks.prompt: Create Revenue Selected Products so the denominator respects slicers but ignores the current visual row.
chunks.solution: Revenue Selected Products = CALCULATE([Total Revenue], ALLSELECTED(Product))
hints: This is useful for visual percentages.

chunks.title: Compute share of selected revenue
chunks.prompt: Create Product Revenue Share using DIVIDE so blank or zero denominators do not break the report.
chunks.solution: Product Revenue Share = DIVIDE([Total Revenue], [Revenue Selected Products])
hints: Use the selected-products denominator from the previous chunk.

chunks.title: Declare an order-date sales measure
chunks.prompt: Write Total Sales using the active OrderDate relationship.
chunks.solution: Total Sales = SUM(Sales[SalesAmount])
hints: The active relationship handles OrderDate automatically.

chunks.title: Activate the ship-date relationship
chunks.prompt: Write Sales by Ship Date using USERELATIONSHIP between Date[Date] and Sales[ShipDate].
chunks.solution: Sales by Ship Date = CALCULATE([Total Sales], USERELATIONSHIP(Date[Date], Sales[ShipDate]))
hints: The inactive relationship is temporarily activated for this measure.

chunks.title: Create a distinct customer count
chunks.prompt: Write a measure that counts unique customers at the fact-table grain.
chunks.solution: Customers = DISTINCTCOUNT(Sales[CustomerKey])
hints: Use DISTINCTCOUNT for unique customer keys.
Do not count rows unless each row is exactly one customer.

chunks.title: Calculate revenue per customer
chunks.prompt: Write Revenue per Customer using your Total Sales and Customers measures.
chunks.solution: Revenue per Customer = DIVIDE([Total Sales], [Customers])

chunks.title: Import pandas and create a dataframe
chunks.prompt: Import pandas as pd and create a dataframe named orders from the provided dictionary.
chunks.solution:
import pandas as pd
orders = pd.DataFrame(raw_orders)

chunks.title: Fill missing revenue
chunks.prompt: Replace missing revenue values with 0 and store the result back in orders["revenue"].
chunks.solution: orders["revenue"] = orders["revenue"].fillna(0)
hints: Assign the cleaned column back to the same column name.

chunks.title: Create a high-value flag
chunks.prompt: Add a boolean column named high_value that is True when revenue is at least 300.
chunks.solution: orders["high_value"] = orders["revenue"] >= 300

chunks.title: Summarize revenue by segment
chunks.prompt: Create segment_summary with total revenue and order count by segment.
chunks.solution: segment_summary = orders.groupby("segment").agg(total_revenue=("revenue", "sum"), order_count=("order_id", "count")).reset_index()
hints: Named aggregations make the output readable.

worksheets.title: SQL Joins and Aggregation for Flight Data

chunks.title: Select the flight grain
chunks.prompt: Write a query that returns flight_id, carrier, origin, destination, and arrival_delay from flights.
chunks.solution:
SELECT flight_id, carrier, origin, destination, arrival_delay
FROM flights;
hints: Start by naming the columns you need.

chunks.title: Filter delayed flights
chunks.prompt: Return only flights with arrival_delay greater than 15 minutes.

chunks.title: Join airline names
chunks.prompt: Join flights to airlines so the output includes airline_name.
chunks.solution:
SELECT f.flight_id, a.airline_name, f.origin, f.destination, f.arrival_delay
FROM flights AS f
JOIN airlines AS a
  ON f.carrier = a.carrier;
hints: Join on the shared carrier code.

chunks.title: Average delay by airline
chunks.prompt: Calculate average arrival delay and flight count by airline_name, sorted from highest delay to lowest.
chunks.solution:
SELECT a.airline_name,
       AVG(f.arrival_delay) AS avg_arrival_delay,
       COUNT(*) AS flight_count
FROM flights AS f
JOIN airlines AS a
  ON f.carrier = a.carrier
GROUP BY a.airline_name
ORDER BY avg_arrival_delay DESC;
hints: ORDER BY can use the alias.

chunks.title: Import the text-mining tools
chunks.prompt: Import train_test_split, TfidfVectorizer, LogisticRegression, and accuracy_score.
chunks.solution:
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score
hints: Logistic regression is a solid baseline classifier.

chunks.title: Split text and labels
chunks.prompt: Split df["text"] and df["label"] into train/test sets with test_size=.25 and random_state=42.
chunks.solution: X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(df["text"], df["label"], test_size=0.25, random_state=42)
hints: Keep names X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test.

chunks.title: Vectorize the documents
chunks.prompt: Fit a TfidfVectorizer on the training text and transform both training and test text.
chunks.solution:
vectorizer = TfidfVectorizer(stop_words="english", min_df=2)
X_train_vec = vectorizer.fit_transform(X_train)
X_test_vec = vectorizer.transform(X_test)
hints: Transform the test text with the fitted vectorizer.

chunks.title: Train and evaluate a classifier
chunks.prompt: Train LogisticRegression and calculate accuracy on the test set.
chunks.solution:
model = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)
model.fit(X_train_vec, y_train)
preds = model.predict(X_test_vec)
accuracy = accuracy_score(y_test, preds)

chunks.solution:
import pandas as pd
story = pd.DataFrame(columns=["section", "audience_question", "evidence_needed"])
hints: Start with empty columns so you can append rows later.

chunks.title: Add the decision row
chunks.prompt: Add one row describing the decision the audience needs to make.
chunks.solution: story.loc[len(story)] = ["Decision", "What choice needs to be made?", "A clear recommendation and tradeoff summary"]

chunks.title: Import Gurobi and create a model
chunks.prompt: Import gurobipy as gp, import GRB, and create a model named model.
chunks.solution:
import gurobipy as gp
from gurobipy import GRB

model = gp.Model("product_mix")
hints: Most Gurobi examples use gp as the alias.
GRB stores constants such as MAXIMIZE.

chunks.title: Add decision variables
chunks.prompt: Create nonnegative variables x and y for two products.
chunks.solution:
x = model.addVar(lb=0, name="x")
y = model.addVar(lb=0, name="y")
hints: Name variables so output is readable.

chunks.title: Add resource constraints
chunks.prompt: Add constraints: 2x + y <= 100 and x + 3y <= 120.
chunks.solution:
model.addConstr(2 * x + y <= 100, name="labor")
model.addConstr(x + 3 * y <= 120, name="materials")
hints: Names help interpret shadow prices and diagnostics.

chunks.title: Set objective and solve
chunks.prompt: Maximize 40x + 50y and optimize the model.
chunks.solution:
model.setObjective(40 * x + 50 * y, GRB.MAXIMIZE)
model.optimize()
hints: Use GRB.MAXIMIZE for a maximization problem.
Call optimize() after variables, constraints, and objective exist.

worksheets.title: Transportation and Assignment Model Pattern
sourceRefs: Classes /Fall 2025/ISA 634/Exam 2/Topic 1. Transportation and Assignment Problems/05 - Transportation & Assignment Problems (1).pdf

chunks.title: Define supply, demand, and costs
chunks.prompt: Create dictionaries for supply, demand, and shipping cost keyed by origin/destination.
hints: Use small dictionaries first; scale later.

chunks.title: Create shipment variables
chunks.prompt: Create one nonnegative decision variable for every origin-destination pair.
chunks.solution: ship = model.addVars(cost.keys(), lb=0, name="ship")
hints: addVars can take the cost keys directly.
Each variable represents flow on an arc.

chunks.title: Add supply constraints
chunks.prompt: For each origin, ensure total outbound shipments do not exceed supply.
chunks.solution:
for i in supply:
    model.addConstr(gp.quicksum(ship[i, j] for j in demand) <= supply[i], name=f"supply_{i}")
hints: Sum all destinations for each origin.

chunks.title: Add demand constraints and objective
chunks.prompt: Meet each destination demand and minimize total shipping cost.
chunks.solution:
for j in demand:
    model.addConstr(gp.quicksum(ship[i, j] for i in supply) >= demand[j], name=f"demand_{j}")

model.setObjective(gp.quicksum(cost[i, j] * ship[i, j] for i, j in cost), GRB.MINIMIZE)
model.optimize()
hints: The objective multiplies cost by flow.

worksheets.title: Gradient Descent from Scratch
sourceRefs: Classes /Spring 2026/ISA 630/Module 1_ [Gradients, Regularization]/[1] Learning, Loss Functions, Cost Functions, Gradients /Loss, Cost, and Gradients.ipynb

chunks.title: Import NumPy and set training data
chunks.prompt: Import numpy and create arrays X and y for a tiny linear regression example.
chunks.solution:
import numpy as np

X = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4], dtype=float)
y = np.array([3, 5, 7, 9], dtype=float)
hints: Use dtype=float so gradient math is smooth.

chunks.title: Initialize parameters
chunks.prompt: Initialize weight w, bias b, and learning_rate.
chunks.solution:
w = 0.0
b = 0.0
learning_rate = 0.01
hints: The learning rate controls step size.

chunks.title: Compute predictions and mean squared error
chunks.prompt: Calculate predictions and the mean squared error loss.
chunks.solution:
preds = w * X + b
loss = np.mean((preds - y) ** 2)
hints: Linear prediction is w * X + b.
Mean squared error averages squared residuals.

chunks.title: Take one gradient descent step
chunks.prompt: Compute gradients for w and b, then update both parameters.
chunks.solution:
dw = np.mean(2 * (preds - y) * X)
db = np.mean(2 * (preds - y))

w = w - learning_rate * dw
b = b - learning_rate * db
hints: Gradients point uphill; subtract them to reduce loss.
The bias gradient does not multiply by X.

chunks.title: Import Keras building blocks
chunks.prompt: Import Sequential, Conv2D, MaxPooling2D, Flatten, and Dense.
chunks.solution:
from tensorflow.keras.models import Sequential
from tensorflow.keras.layers import Conv2D, MaxPooling2D, Flatten, Dense
hints: Sequential is enough for a first image classifier.

chunks.title: Start the model with a convolution block
chunks.prompt: Create a Sequential model with a Conv2D layer and MaxPooling2D layer for 64x64 RGB images.
chunks.solution:
model = Sequential([
    Conv2D(32, (3, 3), activation="relu", input_shape=(64, 64, 3)),
    MaxPooling2D((2, 2)),
])

chunks.title: Add dense classification layers
chunks.prompt: Flatten the convolution output and add a hidden Dense layer plus a sigmoid output layer.
chunks.solution:
model.add(Flatten())
model.add(Dense(64, activation="relu"))
model.add(Dense(1, activation="sigmoid"))
hints: Flatten bridges convolution layers to dense layers.

chunks.title: Compile the classifier
chunks.prompt: Compile the model for binary classification using Adam and accuracy.
chunks.solution: model.compile(optimizer="adam", loss="binary_crossentropy", metrics=["accuracy"])
hints: accuracy is an easy first metric, not the only metric.

chunks.title: Create a numeric series
chunks.prompt: Import numpy and create a simple array named series.
chunks.solution:
import numpy as np

series = np.array([10, 12, 13, 15, 18, 21, 23, 25, 28, 30], dtype=float)

chunks.title: Set window and horizon
chunks.prompt: Set window_size to 3 and horizon to 1.
chunks.solution:
window_size = 3
horizon = 1
hints: Window size is how much history the model sees.
Horizon is how far ahead it predicts.

chunks.title: Build input/output windows
chunks.prompt: Loop through the series and build X windows with matching y next-step values.
chunks.solution:
X, y = [], []
for i in range(len(series) - window_size - horizon + 1):
    X.append(series[i:i + window_size])
    y.append(series[i + window_size + horizon - 1])
hints: Each X row is a slice of prior values.
The y value is the future target after the window.

chunks.title: Convert windows into model arrays
chunks.prompt: Convert X and y to NumPy arrays and reshape X for an RNN with one feature.
chunks.solution:
X = np.array(X).reshape(-1, window_size, 1)
y = np.array(y)
hints: RNN input shape is samples x timesteps x features.
Here there is one feature per timestep.

chunks.title: Import Spark functions
chunks.prompt: Import col, avg, and count from pyspark.sql.functions.
chunks.solution: from pyspark.sql.functions import col, avg, count

chunks.title: Filter active accounts
chunks.prompt: Create active_accounts by filtering accounts where status equals "active".
chunks.solution: active_accounts = accounts.filter(col("status") == "active")

chunks.title: Aggregate by segment
chunks.prompt: Create segment_metrics with count and average revenue by segment.
chunks.solution:
segment_metrics = active_accounts.groupBy("segment").agg(
    count("*").alias("account_count"),

chunks.title: Sort distributed results

chunks.solution: segment_metrics = segment_metrics.orderBy(col("avg_revenue").desc())

chunks.title: Import ALS and evaluator
chunks.prompt: Import ALS and RegressionEvaluator from Spark ML.
chunks.solution:
from pyspark.ml.recommendation import ALS
from pyspark.ml.evaluation import RegressionEvaluator
hints: RMSE is often used for rating prediction.

chunks.title: Create the ALS model
chunks.prompt: Create an ALS model using userId, itemId, rating, and coldStartStrategy="drop".
chunks.solution: als = ALS(userCol="userId", itemCol="itemId", ratingCol="rating", coldStartStrategy="drop")
hints: Cold-start rows can produce NaN predictions.

chunks.title: Fit and predict
chunks.prompt: Fit ALS on train_df and predict ratings for test_df.
chunks.solution:
als_model = als.fit(train_df)
predictions = als_model.transform(test_df)

chunks.prompt: Evaluate predictions using RMSE with rating as the label and prediction as the prediction column.
chunks.solution:
evaluator = RegressionEvaluator(metricName="rmse", labelCol="rating", predictionCol="prediction")
rmse = evaluator.evaluate(predictions)
hints: Use the same label column used during training.

chunks.title: Create a reviewed retrieval table
chunks.prompt: Create a dataframe with query, retrieved_doc, relevant, and answer_supported columns.
chunks.solution:
import pandas as pd
reviews = pd.DataFrame(columns=["query", "retrieved_doc", "relevant", "answer_supported"])
hints: A simple review table is enough to start.
Separate retrieval relevance from answer support.

chunks.title: Add a reviewed query
chunks.prompt: Append one row for a query where the retrieved document is relevant and supports the answer.
chunks.solution: reviews.loc[len(reviews)] = ["What is feature leakage?", "model_validation_notes", True, True]
hints: A relevant doc should actually answer the query.

chunks.title: Calculate context recall proxy
chunks.prompt: Calculate the share of reviewed queries where relevant is True.
chunks.solution: context_recall_proxy = reviews["relevant"].mean()
hints: True averages as 1, False averages as 0.
This is a simple proxy, not a full benchmark.

chunks.title: Calculate answer support rate
chunks.prompt: Calculate the share of reviewed queries where answer_supported is True.
chunks.solution: answer_support_rate = reviews["answer_supported"].mean()
hints: Support means the answer can be traced to retrieved content.
This helps separate retrieval failure from generation failure.

chunks.title: Create treatment summaries
chunks.prompt: Create a dataframe with visitors and conversions for variants A and B.
hints: Each row is one experimental variant.
Keep counts aggregated for this worksheet.

chunks.title: Calculate conversion rates
chunks.prompt: Add a conversion_rate column.
chunks.solution: ab["conversion_rate"] = ab["conversions"] / ab["visitors"]
hints: Conversion rate is conversions divided by visitors.

chunks.title: Calculate lift
chunks.prompt: Calculate the relative lift of B compared with A.
chunks.solution:
rate_a = ab.loc[ab["variant"] == "A", "conversion_rate"].iloc[0]
rate_b = ab.loc[ab["variant"] == "B", "conversion_rate"].iloc[0]
lift = (rate_b - rate_a) / rate_a
hints: Relative lift divides the difference by the baseline.

chunks.title: Run a two-proportion z-test
chunks.prompt: Use statsmodels proportions_ztest to test whether conversion rates differ.
chunks.solution:
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportions_ztest

count = ab["conversions"].to_numpy()
nobs = ab["visitors"].to_numpy()
z_stat, p_value = proportions_ztest(count, nobs)

worksheets.title: Epsilon-Greedy Bandit Simulation
sourceRefs: Classes /Spring 2026/ISA 633/6. Module 5_ Multi-arm bandits/Notes/Introduction to Multi Arm Bandits.Rmd

chunks.title: Initialize reward tracking
chunks.prompt: Create arrays for arm counts and estimated values for three arms.
chunks.solution:
import numpy as np

n_arms = 3
counts = np.zeros(n_arms)
values = np.zeros(n_arms)
epsilon = 0.1
hints: counts tracks how often each arm is pulled.

chunks.title: Choose an arm
chunks.prompt: Choose a random arm with probability epsilon, otherwise choose the arm with the highest estimated value.

chunks.title: Simulate a reward
chunks.prompt: Given true_rates, simulate a binary reward for the selected arm.
chunks.solution: reward = 1 if np.random.random() < true_rates[arm] else 0
hints: Higher true rate means success is more likely.

chunks.title: Update the selected arm estimate
chunks.prompt: Increment the selected arm count and update its running average reward.
chunks.solution:
counts[arm] += 1
values[arm] = values[arm] + (reward - values[arm]) / counts[arm]
hints: This is an online mean update.

worksheets.title: Difference-in-Differences Setup
sourceRefs: Classes /Spring 2026/ISA 633/10. Module 8_ Causal Inference/rmd notes/Introduction to Causal Inference.Rmd

chunks.title: Create indicator columns
chunks.prompt: Create treated, post, and treated_post columns in df.
chunks.solution:
df["treated"] = (df["group"] == "treated").astype(int)
df["post"] = (df["period"] == "post").astype(int)
df["treated_post"] = df["treated"] * df["post"]
hints: The interaction is treated times post.

chunks.title: Fit the DiD regression
chunks.prompt: Use statsmodels to regress outcome on treated, post, and treated_post.
chunks.solution:
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

model = smf.ols("outcome ~ treated + post + treated_post", data=df).fit()
hints: The interaction coefficient is the DiD estimate.

chunks.title: Extract the treatment effect estimate
chunks.prompt: Store the treated_post coefficient in did_effect.
chunks.solution: did_effect = model.params["treated_post"]
hints: params is indexed by coefficient name.
treated_post is the estimated causal contrast under assumptions.

chunks.title: Summarize uncertainty
chunks.prompt: Store the p-value and confidence interval for treated_post.
chunks.solution:
did_p_value = model.pvalues["treated_post"]
did_ci = model.conf_int().loc["treated_post"]
hints: conf_int() returns lower and upper bounds.
